items.prompt: In the baseline, updatePigBatch ran pigBatches.map((item) => (item.id === batch.id ? batch : item)) and then saved. What happened when the batch id was stale?
items.answer: The map returned an array equal to the original, storage was rewritten with it and the state setter accepted it - the update reported success while changing nothing
distractors: map threw a TypeError because no element matched
The stale batch was appended to the end of the array
AsyncStorage rejected the write because the content was unchanged
items.explanation: A map answers 'what would the array look like if this id were present', not 'did the resource exist'.

items.prompt: After the change, updatePigBatch is called with an id that is not in pigBatches. What is the sequence of effects?
items.answer: findIndex returns -1, replaceRecordById throws, and neither savePigBatches nor setPigBatches runs
distractors: The helper returns the original array and the save is skipped as a no-op
savePigBatches runs first, then the helper throws during setPigBatches
The helper inserts the batch as a new record, converting the update to an add
items.explanation: Valid id: index found, new array, storage write, state update. Missing id: throw, no write, no state change.

items.prompt: Why does replaceRecordById use findIndex and then map, instead of copying the array and assigning copy[index] = replacement?
items.answer: The baseline replaced every matching id; the shortcut would replace only the first duplicate and change that contract
distractors: Index assignment mutates the original array passed in
map is faster than index assignment for arrays of objects
findIndex alone cannot detect a missing id
items.explanation: The change was meant to add a guard without altering behavior; test 3 (duplicate-id replacement) fails with the shortcut.

items.prompt: Update now throws for a missing id. Why does deletePigBatch still silently succeed when the id is already absent?
items.answer: A repeated delete expresses the same intent and reaches the same end state, so staying idempotent is safe for a UI retry
distractors: Because filter cannot detect whether anything was removed
Because deletes are rolled back by AsyncStorage if nothing changed
It is an oversight; the rubric requires delete to throw as well
items.explanation: Silently accepting absence on update reports success while overwriting nothing; on delete the outcome is what the user asked for.

items.prompt: Two context callbacks holding different copies of the sales array each call saveList. What is the result?
items.answer: Last writer wins: saveList replaces the whole collection with one setItem, so the earlier write is overwritten
distractors: AsyncStorage merges the two arrays by record id
The second write fails because the key is locked by the first
replaceRecordById detects the conflict and throws
items.explanation: The helper is a local state rule, not a database transaction; whole-array writes have no concurrency control.

items.prompt: A call to replaceRecordById succeeds. Which claim does that establish?
items.answer: At least one record with the replacement's id existed in the supplied array - not that ids are unique or that the array is the latest persisted one
distractors: Exactly one record had that id, so the replacement was unambiguous
The array matched what is currently stored in AsyncStorage
The caller is authorized to modify the record
items.explanation: Keeping exists, unique and current separate lets a reviewer tell an identity error from a persistence or concurrency error.

items.prompt: replaceRecordById throws synchronously inside the async updateSale callback. What does the caller observe?
items.answer: A rejected promise, produced before the first await, so the storage write never starts
distractors: An uncaught exception that crashes the React Native app
A resolved promise, because async functions swallow synchronous throws
A rejection only after saveSales finishes writing
items.explanation: Inside an async function a throw becomes a rejection; because it happens before the await, a missing resource and a storage failure never share a success path.

items.prompt: The user edits a sale whose record was deleted elsewhere. What does SaleFormScreen show?
items.answer: The generic 'The sale could not be saved. Please try again.' - the bare catch discards the helper's 'was not found' message, and retrying cannot succeed
distractors: Record '<id>' was not found., the helper's own error text
Nothing; the form navigates back as if the save succeeded
A prompt offering to re-create the sale as a new record
items.explanation: catch without binding the error makes identity, validation and storage failures indistinguishable, and 'try again' is misleading here.

items.prompt: Adding a sale empties its batch, so the screen awaits addSale and then updatePigBatch with status sold_out. The second write rejects. What happens if the user retries?
items.answer: A duplicate sale: the first sale was already persisted, the alert claimed it was not saved, and the retry creates a new id
distractors: Nothing duplicates, because addSale is idempotent by sale id
The first sale is rolled back automatically by AsyncStorage
The retry fails with 'was not found' because the batch is sold out
items.explanation: Nothing spans the two AsyncStorage keys; one failure message covers two sequential writes.

items.answer: No - it is an identity check in a single-user, on-device app; there is no authorization or tenant boundary in the context
distractors: Yes - it rejects records belonging to another user
Yes - it verifies the record against validation.ts rules before replacing
Partly - it checks ownership only for sales and pig batches
items.explanation: Data validation lives in validation.ts; identity validation belongs in collection.ts. Neither is access control.

items.prompt: A callback's closure still holds an array containing a record that was deleted since. Does the helper stop the update?
items.answer: No - the id is present in the captured array, so the guard passes and the write resurrects the deleted record
distractors: Yes - the helper re-reads storage before checking the id
Yes - React always refreshes closures before an async callback runs
No - but AsyncStorage rejects writes containing deleted ids
items.explanation: Preventing that needs a version check or a re-read before write, not a stronger helper.

items.prompt: records = [a, b]; replaceRecordById(records, b2) returns result. Which statement is true?
items.answer: result is a new array [a, b2] in the same order, and result[0] is the very same object as records[0]
distractors: result === records, because b was replaced in place
result[0] is a deep clone of a, so later edits to a do not affect it
result is [b2, a], because replacements are moved to the front
items.explanation: The helper builds a fresh array without mutating its input; unchanged records keep their references - shallow, not deep, immutability.

items.front: What does replaceRecordById (src/utils/collection.ts:1-8) do for a match, for a missing id, and what boundary does it make explicit?
items.back: Match: returns a new array with every record of that id replaced. Missing: throws 'Record <id> was not found.' The boundary is resource existence - the caller can no longer run a storage writer after a false update.

items.front: Rubric for accepting the update-guard change (helper imported at src/context/AppDataContext.tsx:27): what must be true, and which patches are rejected?
items.back: Every update callback uses the same helper (1 import + 6 calls), valid replacement preserves order, missing identity throws before any await, add/delete unchanged, tests import production source. Reject patches that insert a missing update, convert update to add, or catch the error and report success.

items.front: Finding F2: SaleFormScreen.tsx:97-99 rebuilds nextSales with sales.map((sale) => sale.id === nextSale.id ? nextSale : sale). Why is it flagged even though it is harmless today?
items.back: It re-implements the old silent map in the screen. It is safe only because updateSale already threw for a missing id; it duplicates the policy the helper was meant to own, so a future change can drift.

items.front: One fix direction for the two-write sale save is to stop persisting a derived status. What already derives sold_out (src/utils/calculations.ts:312)?
items.back: The display calculation derives status from quantity: closed stays closed, a current quantity of 0 shows sold_out, otherwise the stored status. If display already derives it, the second updatePigBatch write - and its partial-failure window - could be dropped.
